t.1.1: In the northern quarter there is the king of mountains named Himālaya, whose very soul is divine; plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod of the earth.
t.1.2: Him all the mountains made their calf, and with Meru, skilled in milking, standing as the milker, they milked from the earth, as Pṛthu had taught, shining gems and mighty herbs.
t.1.3: For him, the source of countless gems, the snow did not become a destroyer of his beauty; for a single flaw sinks from sight amid a host of virtues, as the mark on the moon is lost among its rays.
t.1.4: And on its peaks it bears a wealth of minerals that furnishes the adornments for the amorous graces of the Apsarases, its red hues parted by scattered fragments of cloud, like an untimely twilight.
t.1.5: The Siddhas, having enjoyed the shade of the clouds that drift about its girdle-line, a shade that falls on the slopes below, are then harassed by the rains and take refuge on its sunlit peaks.
t.1.6: There, even without seeing the blood-red tracks washed away by the trickling snowmelt, the Kirātas know the path of lions that have slain elephants by the pearls dropped from the hollows of their claws.
t.1.7: There, the birch-bark leaves, red like the spots on an elephant and inscribed with letters in liquid mineral dye, come into use as love letters written by the lovely Vidyādhara maidens.
t.1.9: Where the fragrance released from the sarala trees, as their milky sap flows when elephants rub against them to relieve the itching of their temples, perfumes the mountain slopes.
t.1.8: He who, filling the hollows of the bamboo reeds with the wind that rises from the mouths of his caves, wishes, as it were, to become the giver of the keynote for the Kiṃnaras who are about to sing.
t.1.10: Where, at night, the luminous herbs, their radiance cast upon the laps of cave-dwellings, become lamps of love needing no fill of oil for the forest-dwellers who keep company with their women.
t.1.13: The yak-cows, with the fans of their tails, white as the rays of the moon, whose splendour spreads as they flick their tails this way and that, make meaningful his title, Girirāja, king of mountains.
t.1.11: There, even though the snow on the path has hardened into stone and stings their toes and heels, the horse-faced women, wearied by hips and breasts heavy to carry, do not break their slow and stately gait.
t.1.12: He shelters from the sun the darkness that lies hidden in his caves, as though afraid of the day; surely the lofty-headed feel a sense of 'this is mine' toward even a lowly one who has come to them for refuge, just as they would toward the noble.
t.1.14: There, when the Kiṃpuruṣa women are abashed at having their garments snatched away, clouds whose masses happen to hang at the doorways of the cave-dwellings become curtains for them.
t.1.15: There the Kirātas, who have been tracking deer, enjoy the wind that bears the spray of the Bhāgīrathī's waterfalls, again and again shakes the deodars, and parts the plumes of the peacocks.
t.1.16: Its summit-grown lotuses, those left over after the Saptarṣis have plucked them with their hands, are awakened by the sun, which circles below and opens them with its upward-turned rays.
t.1.17: Perceiving that he was the source of the requisites of sacrifice, and that his strength was able to bear the earth, Prajāpati himself established for him the sovereignty over the mountains, with a share in the sacrifice allotted to it.
t.1.18: He, the friend of Meru, who knew the established order, duly wedded, for the continuance of his lineage, Menā, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, a bride worthy of honour even from the sages and well suited to himself.
t.1.19: Then, in the course of time, when the pleasures of love befitting their own forms had begun between the two, the queen of the king of mountains, bearing a youth delightful to the mind, conceived a child.
t.1.20: She gave birth to Maināka, fit to be enjoyed by the wives of the Nāgas, who had bound himself in friendship with the ocean, and who, even when Vṛtra's foe, the cutter of mountains' wings, was enraged, never came to know the pain of wounds from the thunderbolt.
t.1.21: Then Satī, daughter of Dakṣa and former wife of Bhava, being virtuous, cast off her body through yoga, driven to it by her father's insult, and approached that wife of the mountain for the sake of rebirth.
t.1.22: That auspicious maiden was begotten by the lord of the mountains upon her, who was steadfast in devotion, just as prosperity is brought forth by the virtue of energy in statecraft kept unimpaired through right application.
t.1.23: With the quarters of the sky serene, the winds free of dust, and a shower of flowers falling right after the sound of conches, that day of her birth brought happiness to all embodied beings, both the stationary and the moving.
t.1.24: Through that daughter, ringed with a shimmering halo of radiance, the mother shone all the more brightly, just as the land of Vidūra shines with a shoot of gemstone sprung up at the sound of the new clouds' thunder.
t.1.25: Growing day by day, she, having had her rising like the crescent of the moon, nourished ever new distinctions full of loveliness, just as the crescent nourishes successive digits that hold moonlight within them.
t.1.26: Her kinsfolk called her, so dear to her kin, by the name Pārvatī, drawn from her lineage; later, when her mother forbade her from austerity with the cry “U mā,” “Oh, do not,” the fair-faced maiden came to bear the name Umā.
t.1.27: Though the mountain lord had sons, his gaze never tired of looking at that child; for though spring bears countless flowers, the swarm of bees clings with special fondness to the mango.
t.1.29: In her childhood, standing in the midst of her friends, she played again and again with little altars of sand on the banks of the Mandākinī, with balls and with dolls, as though savoring to the full the delight of play.
t.1.28: As a lamp is by a flame great in radiance, as the path to heaven is by the three-pathed river, as a wise man is by refined speech, so was he both purified and adorned by her.
t.1.31: Then she reached the age beyond childhood, an adornment of her slender, graceful body that needed no gathering, a cause of intoxication not called wine, and a weapon of Kāma other than flowers.
t.1.30: As rows of swans come to the Gaṅgā in autumn, and as their own radiance comes to the great herbs at night, so, when the time for her instruction came, the knowledge of her former birth came to her, steadfast in what she was taught.
t.1.32: Like a painting brought out by the painter's brush, like a lotus opened by the rays of the sun, her body, shapely and beautiful in its perfect symmetry, became clearly defined by fresh youth.
t.1.33: Her two feet, which with the radiance of the nails of their raised big toes seemed to pour forth a red glow wherever they were set down, brought to the earth the beauty of land-lotuses, a beauty that moved from place to place.
t.1.34: She, her limbs gently bowed, was taught, as it were, by the royal swans in gaits whose steps were graced with playful charm, for they were eager for a lesson in return and wished to acquire from her the tinkling of her anklets.
t.1.36: Though the trunks of lordly elephants and the finest plantain stems have won renown in the world for their ample, rounded form, they fell outside comparison with her thighs, the former because of the roughness of their skin, the latter because of their unrelieved coldness.
t.1.35: When the Creator had fashioned her lovely shanks, rounded, tapering in due order and not overlong, it was as if, in the work of forming her remaining limbs, his effort went into producing loveliness anew.
t.1.37: Surely the beauty of the blameless one's hips, the place of her girdle-string, may be inferred from this alone: that later Giriśa set them upon his lap, a place no other woman could aspire to.
t.1.38: Her slender line of new down, passing beyond the knot of her garment and entering the deep hollow of her navel, shone like the radiance of the dark central gem of her girdle.
t.1.39: The young girl, her waist slender as the narrow middle of a sacrificial altar, bore at her waist a lovely triple fold, like a staircase set there by fresh youth for Kāma to climb.
t.1.40: The pale pair of breasts of the lotus-eyed maiden grew so full, pressing against each other, that in the middle of that dark-tipped pair not even the width of a lotus-fiber thread could be found.
t.1.42: Between her throat, gracefully curved above her breasts, and the necklace of perfectly round pearls, since each lent beauty to the other, the relation of ornament and thing adorned became shared by both.
t.1.41: Her two arms, I imagine, surpassed even the śirīṣa flower in delicacy, those arms that Makaradhvaja, though he had been defeated, made into nooses about Hara's neck.
t.1.43: When she goes to the moon, Lakṣmī does not enjoy the virtues of the lotus, and when she dwells in the lotus she does not enjoy the moon's splendor. But fickle Lakṣmī, on reaching Umā's face, found a delight that rested in both at once.
t.1.44: If a flower were set upon a fresh red shoot, or a pearl were placed on gleaming coral, then it might imitate her bright smile, whose radiance spread across her copper-red lips.
t.1.45: When she, whose speech was noble, spoke in a voice that seemed to flow with nectar, even the female cuckoo sounded harsh to the listener, like a lute with faulty strings being struck.
t.1.46: That unsteady, tremulous glance of the long-eyed maiden, no different from blue lotuses tossed by the wind: was it learned by her from the doe-eyed deer, or was it learned from her by the does?
t.1.47: The loveliness of her brows, curving in gentle arching lines, seemed as if drawn with a collyrium-pencil; seeing that beauty so skilled in playful grace, Anaṅga gave up his pride in the beauty of his own bow.
t.1.48: If shame could dwell in the minds of animals, then surely the yak-cows, on beholding that mass of hair of the daughter of the King of Mountains, would slacken their fondness for their own tails.
t.1.49: With great effort the Creator of the universe fashioned her from the whole assemblage of things that serve as standards of comparison, each set in its proper place, as if from a desire to behold all beauty gathered in one place.
t.1.50: Once, it is said, Nārada, who roams at will, saw that maiden at her father's side and foretold that she would become the sole bride of Hara, one who through love would claim half of his body.
t.1.51: Therefore, even though she had reached the full ripeness of youth, her father remained with all desire for any other bridegroom turned away; for no luminous powers other than fire are worthy of the oblation purified by sacred mantras.
t.1.52: For the Mountain could not bring himself to make the God of gods, who had not asked for her, accept his daughter; a good man, fearing his request might be refused, remains indifferent even in a matter he desires.
t.1.53: From the very moment when she of the lovely teeth cast off her body in a former birth out of anger at Dakṣa, the Lord of Creatures, Paśupati, freed from all attachment, remained without a wife.
t.1.55: The Gaṇas, wearing nameru blossoms as ear-ornaments and clad in birch-bark garments soft to the touch, their bodies streaked with red arsenic, sat down upon the stone slabs overgrown with rock-moss.
t.1.54: He, the hide-clad one, his self restrained for the sake of austerity, dwelt upon a certain plateau of the Himalaya, where the deodars were sprinkled by the flowing stream of the Gaṅgā, fragrant with musk, and echoing with the singing of kiṃnaras.
t.1.57: There the Eight-Formed One, having laid a fire kindled with sacred fuel, which was itself but another of his own forms, practised austerity out of some unknown desire, though he himself is the bestower of the fruits of austerity.
t.1.56: Scraping the slabs of packed snow with the tips of his hooves, the humped bull, lowing deep in his pride and unable to endure the roar of lions, bellowed aloud, while the terrified gavayas could scarcely bring themselves to look at him.
t.1.58: The lord of mountains honored with a guest-offering him who is beyond all price and is worshipped by the dwellers of heaven. Then he bade his daughter, pure and self-restrained and accompanied by her friends, to attend upon him in worship.
t.1.59: Though she stood as an adversary to his meditation, Giriśa permitted her to serve him; for they alone are truly steadfast whose minds are not perturbed even when a cause of perturbation is present.
t.1.60: Gathering flowers for the offerings, skilled at sweeping the altar, and bringing the water and kuśa grass needed for the prescribed rites, that fair-haired maiden served Giriśa every day, her weariness soothed by the moonbeams shining from his head.
